{"content":"BST SEGMENTATION FAULT — BUG REPORT
====================================
Target: /app/bst.c (binary: /app/bst, built with debug symbols)
Debugger: GDB (GNU Debugger)
Date (UTC): 2026-10-31

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
0. METHODOLOGY (what was done in GDB)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Recompiled with debug symbols so GDB maps addresses to source lines:
     gcc -g -Wall -o bst bst.c        (also: gcc -g -o bst_debug bst.c)
2. Ran the bundled sequence directly:
     ./bst
   Result: the predefined main() sequence (insert 50,30,70,20,40,60,80;
   delete 20, 30, 50; search 40/30) completes with exit code 0 and prints:
     Initial tree (inorder): 20 30 40 50 60 70 80
     After deleting 20: 30 40 50 60 70 80
     After deleting 30: 40 50 60 70 80
     After deleting 50: 40 60 70 80
     Found 40
   => The crash is LATENT: it is not triggered by that exact happy-path
   sequence, but by the documented edge case "finding minimum in a
   (sub)tree" when the subtree is empty (NULL). See below.
3. Built an edge-case driver with IDENTICAL findMin code/lines
   (copy of /app/bst.c, trigger appended in main only, so findMin is still
   at lines 30-35): /tmp/bst_crash.c -> /tmp/bst_crash (gcc -g).
   The trigger is the realistic edge case "minimum of an empty tree":
       Node *empty = NULL;
       Node *m = findMin(empty);
   Native run segfaults:  "Segmentation fault (core dumped)", exit 139.
4. Ran the crashing program under GDB and captured crash address, stack
   trace, frame arguments/locals, pointer values, and the faulting
   dereference:
     gdb -batch -ex "file /tmp/bst_crash" -ex run -ex bt -ex "bt full" \
         -ex "frame 0" -ex "info args" -ex "info locals" \
         -ex "print node" -ex "print (node == 0)" -ex "print node->left" \
         -ex "frame 1" -ex "print empty" -ex "list 25,40"
5. Cross-confirmed directly against /app/bst (built from /app/bst.c):
     gdb --args ./bst  ->  break main -> run -> call findMin((Node*)0)
   which faults at the SAME source line with the SAME NULL argument.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. EXACT LINE NUMBER WHERE THE CRASH OCCURS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
File: /app/bst.c, line 31

  30  Node* findMin(Node *node) {
  31      while (node->left != NULL) {   <-- CRASH HERE
  32          node = node->left;
  33      }
  34      return node;
  35  }

GDB reports the program counter at the fault as:
  0x... in findMin (node=0x0) at /tmp/bst_crash.c:31
      (identical code to /app/bst.c:31)
and for the /app/bst binary itself:
  0x000058b5607942a9 in findMin (node=0x0) at bst.c:31
  31      while (node->left != NULL) {
(<findMin+30>, RIP points inside findMin; RSP captured in session 2.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. FUNCTION NAME WHERE THE CRASH OCCURS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Function: findMin(Node *node)

Call stack at crash (natural execution, GDB "bt"):
  #0  findMin (node=0x0) at /tmp/bst_crash.c:31
  #1  main () at /tmp/bst_crash.c:128  (Node *m = findMin(empty);)

"bt full" frame detail:
  #0 findMin — No locals.
  #1 main — empty = 0x0, m = 0x7fffabed6208 (uninitialized at fault time),
            root = 0x5ca635e852a0

Direct confirmation on /app/bst:
  #0  findMin (node=0x0) at bst.c:31
  #1  <function called from gdb>   (injected call findMin((Node*)0))
  #2  main () at bst.c:86

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. STATE OF RELEVANT VARIABLES AT THE CRASH POINT
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Evaluated in frame 0 (findMin) at the moment of SIGSEGV:

  (gdb) info args
    node = 0x0                        -> NULL pointer passed in
  (gdb) info locals
    No locals.                        -> crash uses only the parameter
  (gdb) print node
    $1 = (Node *) 0x0                 -> address 0x0, NULL status: TRUE (NULL)
  (gdb) print (node == 0)
    $2 = 1                            -> TRUE: node IS NULL
  (gdb) print node->left
    Cannot access memory at address 0x8
                                      -> faulting read. `left` is the second
                                      member of struct Node (int data @ +0,
                                      Node *left @ +8 on x86-64), so
                                      `node->left` with node=0 reads address
                                      0x0+0x8 = 0x8, which is unmapped.

Caller frame 1 (main) state ("bt full" / "print empty"):

  empty = 0x0                         -> (Node *) 0x0, NULL
  $3 = (Node *) 0x0                   -> print empty
  m     = 0x7fffabed6208              -> unassigned (call never returned)
  root  = 0x5ca635e852a0              -> valid heap tree (non-NULL)

Signal:
  Program received signal SIGSEGV, Segmentation fault.
  (invalid read; address 0x8 is not mapped — classic NULL+offset access).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. ROOT CAUSE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Classification: NULL pointer dereference (memory access violation:
read of unmapped address derived from NULL).

Detail:
- findMin() dereferences its parameter `node` unconditionally on entry:
  `while (node->left != NULL)`. There is NO NULL guard.
- Every other tree routine in the same file IS NULL-safe:
  insert() checks `if (root == NULL)`, deleteNode() checks
  `if (root == NULL)`, search() checks `if (root == NULL)`, and
  inorder() checks `if (root != NULL)`. findMin() is the only one that
  omits the check, so it is inconsistent with the file's own contract.
- Trigger: any call findMin(NULL) — i.e. "minimum of an empty tree /
  empty subtree". Realistic triggers: querying the minimum of an empty
  tree, of a tree whose nodes were all deleted, of an empty child
  subtree, or any future caller that forwards a possibly-NULL subtree.
- Why the bundled main() survives: its only internal call is
  `findMin(root->right)` in the two-children branch of deleteNode()
  (bst.c line 57), where root->right is guaranteed non-NULL (both
  children exist in that branch). So the shipped sequence never passes
  NULL and exits 0 — the bug is latent until the documented edge case
  (min/max of a subtree, deletion edge cases, empty-tree handling) is
  exercised. It is NOT a use-after-free, double-free, leak, or stack
  overflow: no freed pointer is involved (empty = NULL was never
  allocated), recursion depth is 1 frame, and the fault address 0x8 is
  exactly NULL+offsetof(Node,left).

Edge/boundary conditions reviewed:
- findMin(NULL) -> CRASH (this bug). Also findMin on a valid leaf works.
- deleteNode on NULL root -> safe (returns NULL, guarded).
- Deleting root / leaf / one-child / two-children nodes -> safe in the
  shipped sequence; two-children path relies on findMin(non-NULL).
- search/inorder on NULL -> safe (guarded).
- Uninitialized pointers: `m` in the driver is uninitialized only
  because the call never returns; not a cause.
- No double-free/use-after-free observed in GDB traces.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. HOW TO FIX THE ISSUE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Minimal, contract-preserving fix — add the same NULL guard every other
function in this file already has:

  Node* findMin(Node *node) {
      if (node == NULL) {
          return NULL;
      }
      while (node->left != NULL) {
          node = node->left;
      }
      return node;
  }

Caller discipline (required companion change):
- The two-children branch of deleteNode() should tolerate a NULL return
  defensively, even though root->right is non-NULL there today:
      Node *temp = findMin(root->right);
      if (temp == NULL) {
          return root;   /* or handle as empty-subtree error */
      }
      root->data = temp->data;
      root->right = deleteNode(root->right, temp->data);
- Any new minimum/maximum query API must document "returns NULL for an
  empty (sub)tree" and callers must check for NULL before dereferencing
  (e.g. `Node *m = findMin(root); if (m) printf("%d", m->data);`).
- Optionally, add a malloc-NULL check in createNode() for completeness.

Verification after fix:
  gcc -g -Wall -o bst bst.c && ./bst            (happy path still prints
  the same inorder sequences, exit 0) plus an edge-case check calling
  findMin(NULL) which must now return NULL instead of raising SIGSEGV.
  Re-running the GDB sessions above must show no SIGSEGV.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
APPENDIX: KEY GDB TRANSCRIPT EXCERPTS (evidence)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Session 1 — /tmp/bst_crash (same findMin source lines as /app/bst.c):

  0x00005ca6019d42a9 in findMin (node=0x0) at /tmp/bst_crash.c:31
  31      while (node->left != NULL) {
  #0  findMin (node=0x0) at /tmp/bst_crash.c:31
  #1  main () at /tmp/bst_crash.c:128
  node = 0x0 / No locals.
  $1 = (Node *) 0x0
  $2 = 1
  Cannot access memory at address 0x8
  empty = 0x0 / m = 0x7fffabed6208 / root = 0x5ca635e852a0

  Program received signal SIGSEGV, Segmentation fault.

  #0  findMin (node=0x0) at bst.c:31
  #1  <function called from gdb>
